# bench_pathtracer

A Monte Carlo path tracer over smallpt's nine-sphere Cornell box, in fixed
point. This is the Move analogue of the EVM `snailtracer` benchmark.

## What it stresses

Signed 128- and 256-bit arithmetic, recursion, and branchy control flow.
Nothing else in the suite exercises wide signed math, and no other kernel mixes
deep integer arithmetic with a decision on almost every step the way a renderer
does.

Concretely, one sample does:

- Nine ray-sphere tests, each an i256 discriminant plus an integer square root.
- A material branch per bounce over three surface types, one of which
  (refraction) splits again on total internal reflection and again on a
  Russian-roulette draw.
- A cosine-weighted hemisphere sample per diffuse bounce, which needs sine,
  cosine, a square root, a cross product and two vector normalisations.

The square root is Newton's method on `u256`, so each call is a fixed number of
256-bit divisions. Nothing here is vectorisable and almost nothing is
predictable, which is the point.

## Initialization

None. The scene is built in memory by `scene()` on every call and `run` touches
no global state, so the package can be published and called immediately.

## Entry points

```move
public fun bench_trace_pixel(x: u64, y: u64, spp: u64, max_depth: u64, seed: u64): u64
public fun bench_render(width: u64, height: u64, spp: u64, max_depth: u64, seed: u64): u64
public entry fun run(_s: &signer, x: u64, y: u64, spp: u64, max_depth: u64, seed: u64, expected: u64)
```

`bench_trace_pixel` traces one pixel of a 1024x768 frame and returns the tone
mapped colour packed as `(r << 16) | (g << 8) | b`, mirroring snailtracer's
`TracePixel`. `bench_render` traces a whole `width` x `height` frame and folds
the packed pixels into a checksum, so it is the same kernel with a much larger
knob. `run` calls `bench_trace_pixel` and aborts with `E_UNEXPECTED` (1) if the
result differs from `expected`.

Pixel `(0, 0)` is the bottom-left corner, as in smallpt.

Every knob, `expected` included, is a runtime argument, so no constant lets the
optimizer fold the kernel away.

## Knobs

| Knob | Meaning | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `spp` | Samples per pixel | Scales cost linearly. Each sample is an independent path. |
| `max_depth` | Hard cap on bounces | Below 6 it dominates; above 6 Russian roulette usually terminates first. `max_depth` of 1 returns the emission of the first hit and traces nothing. |
| `width`, `height` | Frame size, `bench_render` only | Cost is linear in `width * height`. Also changes the camera, so a checksum is not comparable across sizes. |
| `seed` | Base of the per-pixel LCG stream | Changes the sample sequence, not the amount of work, except through the roulette draws. |

Recursion is bounded by `max_depth`, so cost is bounded rather than
distributed. That is the one place this deliberately departs from smallpt,
which relies on Russian roulette alone.

### Choosing a pixel

Like smallpt, this traces paths without sampling the light directly, so a
sample only contributes if a bounce happens to land on the light. The light
covers about 0.6% of the hemisphere seen from the middle of a side wall, so at
low `spp` most pixels come back exactly `0`. That is correct behaviour, not a
bug, but it makes a black pixel a weak `expected` value for `run`: it would
still match after almost any change to the numerics.

Pixels `(168, 574)` and `(856, 574)` land on the left and right walls level
with the light, where a bounce reaches it about 2.5% of the time. They resolve
to a stable colour at 32 samples and are what the tests and the golden value
use. Raising `max_depth` also helps, because every extra bounce is another
chance to find the light.

## Expected values

There is no external reference for this scene in fixed point. The EVM
`snailtracer` renders a different scene and is GPL, and smallpt is floating
point. **The two golden values below were generated by this implementation and
pinned. They are not external references.** They exist so that a refactor that
changes the numerics fails a test instead of passing silently.

| Call | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `bench_trace_pixel(168, 574, 32, 6, 1)` | `8867406`, which unpacks to `(135, 78, 78)` |
| `bench_render(6, 4, 4, 5, 7)` | `200530231` |

Everything else the tests check is verifiable without a golden value:

- `pathtracer_fixed` multiply and divide round-trip, over all four sign
  combinations, with explicit assertions that division truncates toward zero
  rather than flooring.
- `isqrt` against exact squares including `(2^127 - 1)^2`, plus a sweep
  asserting `r*r <= n < (r+1)*(r+1)` and monotonicity.
- Sine and cosine against known angles, and `cos^2 + sin^2 == 1` sampled around
  the whole circle, which fails if the quadrant fold or either series is wrong.
- A ray fired at a sphere of known centre and radius returns the analytic `t`;
  a ray aimed outside the silhouette or behind the origin returns no hit.
- The radius-1e5 wall spheres return the right distance and the right sphere
  index for rays fired along each axis, which is the case where the
  discriminant is a difference of near-equal 1e34 terms.
- A ray fired into the light sphere returns its emission exactly.
- The leftmost column of the frame lands on the red wall and the rightmost on
  the blue one, and a full render of a pixel on each comes back dominant in the
  right channel. A `t`-value test passes on a mirrored or transposed scene; this
  does not.
- Same `(x, y, spp, max_depth, seed)` twice gives the same packed value, and
  changing any one knob changes it, for both entry points.

## Tests

```bash
cargo run -q -p aptos -- move test \
  --package-dir third_party/move/mono-move/benchmarks/bench_pathtracer \
  --skip-fetch-latest-git-deps
```

The Homebrew `aptos` CLI is older than this repo's `move-stdlib` and cannot
compile it. Use the CLI built from this tree.

## Fixed point

Everything is an integer scaled by 1e6, held in `i128`.

`fp_mul` and `fp_div` widen both operands to `i256` before the operation and
narrow afterwards, so an intermediate cannot overflow. Move has no signed
shift, so every scaling is a division, and signed division truncates toward
zero. That is the same rule Solidity's `SDIV` follows, which is why the choice
of `i128` with an explicit divide is a faithful home for a benchmark from the
EVM world, but it is not a shift: for negatives it rounds toward zero where a
shift would round down. `test_division_truncates_toward_zero` pins that.

The ray-sphere discriminant is the one place where naive fixed point falls
apart. For the radius-1e5 wall spheres, `b^2` and `|op|^2 - r^2` are each near
1e34 and agree in their leading four digits, so narrowing either one to 1e6
first would leave about two significant digits in the answer. `dot_raw` keeps
the sum of products at 1e12 without narrowing, the discriminant is assembled at
1e24 in `i256`, and the square root of a value at 1e24 is a value at 1e12 for
free. The result is exact up to a single final division.

Square root is Newton's method on `u256`, seeded by a power of two found with
an unsigned shift ladder. Signed shifts do not exist, but unsigned ones do, and
the radicand is always non-negative. The seed is within a factor of two of the
root, so eight iterations suffice for any `u256` and the cost does not depend
on the input.

Sine and cosine are Taylor series after folding the angle into the first
quadrant, where the last term retained is already below the 1e-6 resolution.

## Provenance

Modeled on [smallpt](https://www.kevinbeason.com/smallpt/) (2008) by Kevin
Beason, which the author released under the MIT license. The scene, the camera,
the tent filter, the three materials, the Russian roulette and the overall
structure of `radiance` follow smallpt. The float-to-fixed-point conversion,
the square root, the trigonometry and the sampling stream are ours.

[snailtracer](https://github.com/karalabe/snailtracer) is GPL-3.0 and this repo
is Apache-2.0. It was read to see which fixed-point conventions it settled on
and to sanity-check ours. No code was copied from it, and none of it appears
here.

## Deviations

From smallpt:

- Fixed point at 1e6 instead of double precision.
- Our own LCG, seeded per pixel, instead of `erand48`. It is the LCG the rest
  of this benchmark suite uses. It is a poor generator with a period of
  1000003, which is fine here: the point is a deterministic, reproducible
  stream, not an unbiased estimate of the rendering equation.
- No 2x2 subpixel subdivision. `spp` is the total sample count for the pixel
  and the tent filter covers the whole pixel, so a given `spp` is four times
  cheaper than smallpt's.
- Gamma 2 instead of 2.2, so the transfer function is the square root already
  needed elsewhere rather than a general `pow`.
- `max_depth` caps the recursion. smallpt has no cap.
- The 1/6-turn constant and similar arguments truncate at 1e-6, so angles are
  a few units off exactly where a float would not be. Visible only in the
  test tolerances.

From snailtracer:

- No triangle mesh and no bounding volume hierarchy. This is the sphere scene
  only.
- The walls are red and blue, which is smallpt's Cornell box. There is no green
  wall.

All three materials are here. Refraction in particular is intact: Snell for the
transmitted direction, total internal reflection, the Schlick approximation,
and the depth-dependent choice between tracing both rays and picking one. It is
the branchiest path in the kernel and dropping it would have cost most of what
this benchmark is for.
